Let's start with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me greet all the people present today, Thursday. As you know, we're going to have the opening statement by Mr. Praljak. I wanted to tell you that we have -- as you know, we have long hearings. There is one and a half hours before the first break. If you feel unwell, if you want an interruption, please tell me so, so that the person who does not feel well can have a rest, a short rest. So do not hesitate to ask me to adjourn the hearing if you need me to do so. Mr. Praljak, you are going to have the floor. It is customary for the person having the floor to be standing up. If you are tired, you can sit down and continue with your opening statement. Do as you please. If you can remain standing for four hours, do so. Otherwise, you're free to sit down and proceed with the opening statement. Lawyers are used to being on their feet for a long time, but other people who are not lawyers may find it more difficult. So it's up to you. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you for your words, Your Honour. I shall sit down only if there are any technical problems. To begin with, I wish to greet Your Honours, all the Defence counsel gathered here, as well as the opposite side, Mr. Scott and his team. Thank you for hearing me today. We have heard Mr. Scott, and when I first appeared before Mr. Antonetti, and I spoke out the following sentence: There is no doubt that Your Honours will reach a just decision if you're presented with the truth. However, the problem of truth in a war is a difficult and complex one. Most often there is a sea of problems arising due to this phenomenon, and the truth is reduced according to the needs of the moment and in order to simplify. Simplification often leads to distortion, especially if many other things are involved in the reduction, if they're not based on the moral imperative of discovering the truth. The Security Council established The Hague Tribunal in order to bring peace to the peoples of the Balkans, as stated by His Honour Judge Antonetti. Peace can obtain only if there is justice. Justice can be achieved only if we have the truth before us. The truth must be founded on facts, not on poor interpretations, not on reduction, not on overlooking important facts. So that using a thousand broken mirrors, extracts out of context, which will lead to a simplification of the highly complex actual situation under conditions when fear, exhaustion, hopelessness reign over people. And just as a conductor conducts a symphonic orchestra, bits can be taken out of the score. Unfortunately, this is what Mr. Scott has done. He has extracted parts of the truth, used quotations out of context, things that are not based in logic in the way he wishes to present. Therefore, I have prepared as briefly as possible but not so briefly as to lose sight of what is essential a presentation showing what happened long before the war, because war, unfortunately, is not the beginning but the climax of a tragedy. It is always the fifth act when death, pain, destruction, rape, and everything else that the civilised world, as Mr. Scott wishes to suggest, has seen in its history more than 10.000 times. After World War II, we have seen it over 300 times, and we still see it on a daily basis today in spite of all the efforts of civilised society to put an end to this. Today, we can list at least 25 serious conflicts for which we do not have a solution. Mr. Mikovic, please show the first slide. In the brief story I will present to you today, I will present you with a brief history of the area settled by the Croats in the Balkans. Please let us see the first slide. Croatia was subject to Venice. It lost its independence in 100 -- in 1102. The way Venice reigned over this territory was the way all conquerors reign. They exploited the natural resources, controlled the sea routes, and for centuries thousands of Croats rode the Venetian valleys. Croatia took over some architecture from Venice. Everything else was pain, looting, and destruction. Let's move on. We entered into a personal union with Hungary in 1102. Systematic centralisation, the imposition of the Hungarian language, taking over the legislation, administration, and financial affairs, putting Rijeka and Medjimurje under direct Hungarian control, taking away the cultural and national identity. All this gave rise to the wish for survival, which led to counter-demonstrations, victims, burnings of flags, the attempts of a nation to survive, according to the natural right of every nation, to remain on its territory and live as other civilised nations do. All this ended only after the end of World War I. Please show the next slide. The Turks arrived in this area in 1463, and in 1493, at the Battle of Krbava, the remainder of the Croatian nobility was killed. Therefore, a lot of what we had in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia was lost. Only a small remnant of the Croatian kingdom was left as well as a part of the Dubrovnik Republic. We had battles led by Nikola Subic-Zrinjski, the Frankopan brothers, and it was in 1593 that we first managed to defeat the Turks at the battle near Sisak, which was the beginning of the downfall of the Turkish Empire. I believe everybody in this courtroom knows what the basic elements of the Turkish rule were: Kidnapping boys who were later made into janissaries, the imposition of huge taxes, forcible conversion to another faith. Throughout this history, when we discussed this in cold blood and rationally, we see it differently, but those who have imagination will hear the cries, the pain, the expulsions from homes, and so on. Next slide, please. Fighting to the left and to the right, you can see on the map how Croatia stretched first a little bit to the left, then a little bit to the right. The remainder of the kingdom of Croatia became ever smaller, ever poorer. It was looted more and more. It was not allowed to develop, to develop its civilisation, it's culture, it's national identity. The Austrians carried out centralisation. They killed Zrinjski, they killed Kristof Frankopan, and of course some of these conquerors of Croatia were better than others but this is not to deny the fact that all of them were very bad for Croatia and brought nothing good to it. Napoleon conquered us in 1805. Please let us have the map. Defeating -- this is it. Napoleon came as far as the River Sava near Zagreb, in Samobor, and the French Revolution and what followed after it meant for Europe the taking off of the shackles of the feudal system, but all that happened in Croatia was that we left part -- that we lost parts of Boka Kotorska after the departure of Napoleon, and the Dubrovnik Republic, which had been free for centuries and where part of where the Croatian cultural identity developed, ceased to exist. When I say that there was heavy fighting between the French and the Russians for the island of Hvar which today has conquered the world public with its beauty, we see what the history of small nations is like. For a full 900 years, there was nothing the Croats could do but suffer the rule of whoever came to this area. With the end of World War I -- please let's have the next slide. With the end of World War I, we have the Italians who occupied or had occupied before that a large part of Istria, many of the Dalmatian islands, Zadar, and the rest. And then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia came into the story. The Italians, of course, mounted the first fascist attack on Croatia. Italy expelled over a hundred thousand Croats and Slovenes from the areas it conquered and gained. It closed over 150 Croatian primary and secondary schools. The Croatian language was thrown out of official use, and the Italian language was introduced, and there was a special court for the protection of the state. And from 1927 to 1932, 106 Croats from Istria were sentenced to a total of 1.124 years in gaol, and five were sentenced to death. The Kingdom of Yugoslavia was created as a result of World War I. Wilson's idea about the right of small nations to self-determination failed, as did many other good intentions concerning the right of nations to independent life, and it failed under the pressure of interests of the great powers. Civilisation was again acting badly as far as Croatia is concerned, because the Serbs were given the war booty. They were presented with Croatia on a silver platter. Their soldiers simply marched through to Croatia, which at the time, and unfortunately, had been part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and was, therefore, now in the possession of the axis powers. In this way, Croatia was again denied its independence. It was simply attached to Serbia as part of its war booty, and there were again expulsions, political trials, the killing of political leaders, for example Stjepan Radic, who was the leader of the Croatian people. Next map, please. On the map we will see now, we shall see what the Kingdom of Serbia was like before World War I and what territory it occupied. Here you see a map of the Kingdom of Serbia and what belonged to the Austro-Hungarian Empire. After that, this entire territory was called the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and a little later it was renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, under the domination of the Serbian King. Wilson's idea of the rights of nations to self-determination thus failed, and Yugoslavia became a country divided into so-called Kotars, administrative units called Kotar. You will see this on the next slide. The territorial organisation of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia is shown on this map. It is divided into administrative units called Kotar, or Srez. Istria and the Dalmatian islands were not part of Yugoslavia at the time. They remained part of fascist Italy. The administrative division into territorial units ran against the political, cultural, and ethnic borders of the time. It represents the beginning of the Greater Serbian idea, which developed or had developed in this area from the end of the 19th century. From 1841, there was systematic political terror. The Assembly was dissolved, election results were not recognised, political activity was banned, political parties were prohibited. Systematic political terror was carried out. Every form of dissatisfaction was brutally punished. Over 25 peasants were killed in a rebellion and a hundred wounded. All opposition politicians, and especially politicians of the Croatian Party of Rights, were persecuted by the regime. From 1929 to 1932, there were 152 political trials; 18 death sentences were handed down, four life sentences, 734 accused were sentenced to 2.348 years of imprisonment. In the same period, 52 members of the Croatian Party of Rights were accused, and of these, 43 were sentenced to 289 years of imprisonment, five to death in absentia, two were sentenced for life, and three were hanged. All this shows that the war in the former Yugoslavia did not begin in 1990. It began in 1918. It was a low intensity war. Throughout this time, Yugoslavia was maintained purely through the political terror of the ruling regimes. In this case, the Serbian regime. It survived only through beatings, murders, punishment. Let's move on. There were rebellions, and there was national struggle for survival. When -- when things became impossible, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was reorganised into banovinas, and then we arrived at one of the key concepts used by Mr. Scott here, the banovina. The banovina was not the beginning of the organisation of Yugoslavia into banovinas as presented by you, because it existed previously, and you have before you the banovinas as they can be seen. There were quite a few of these. And they had nothing really to do with the ethnic and the cultural and economic holes that had existed. It was only after the dictatorship from '29 to '31, the dictatorship of King Aleksandar, when all forms of democracy and democratic political life were abolished in Yugoslavia. He announced that the time had come when there must be no mediators between the King and the people. He abolished the Assembly, the parliament. Then, in order to break up the identity of the peoples living in this area in terms of culture, politics, and so on, he created this division. The resistance of the Croatian people, intellectuals, poets, men of letters, peasants, workers, all men who thought in Croatia was enormous. Therefore, there was -- there were assassinations, the assassination of the King in Marseilles, then the pro-Nazi Yugoslav government was established. And because of the growing political instability, negotiations were opened up about solving the Croatian question within Yugoslavia. The Croatian question was no longer bearable even for those holding power in Belgrade who thought they could deal with things much more simply. It was only then that Cvetkovic-Macek agreement was reached. Cvetkovic was the president of the government of Yugoslavia. Macak was the leader of the Croatian Peasant Party and at that point in time the leader of the Croatian people. And Croats were given certain territorial autonomy so that within the framework of Yugoslavia they could develop the potential, all the potential that a nation has the right to develop. Please let's move on. It was at that time -- no, we don't need that slide. We need the Banovina slide, please. It was then that this map of Banovina emerged, which was so disputed and should represent the basics for analysing everything that was done in this war on behalf of the Croats in Mr. Scott's analysis. I previously said to Mr. Scott that nobody in Croatia would have agreed to Banovina for a simple reason, and you can see on this map what we lose in Banovina. In Banovina, we do not have Istria, we do not have Baranja, we do not have Zadar, we don't have Croatian islands. Banovina was a short-lived and only possible solution at the time to avoid civil war in Yugoslavia. It was short-lived, as I said. And the areas marked in black on this map represent the lost territory of Banovina in Croatia as compared to nowadays, and only territories marked in red were supposed to be some kind of a gain of territory debated so hotly in Croatia, for which Croats are accused. I wanted to say to the Trial Chamber something else. Frequently mention Croatian nationalism as a category which, after the Second World War, was ascribed to Croats as almost their genetic code can be explained by one single fact: The moment the Hungarians drew a border towards Croatia, there was no nationalism on their part. Croats went to Budapest. They wanted to be seen there, to walk there. They had friendly sentiments towards those people the minute they stopped being threatened, stopped feeling threatened by those people. Croats went to Vienna after 400 years of Austrian rule without expressing any of their inherent genetic code. They forgot everything that was done to them. Croats continued travelling to Venetia, to Lido. Croats are friendly to Italians coming to Croatia. Among Croatians, any animosity was purely a result of a threat to their existentialism. We have no nationalism with respect to the French, even though Napoleon ruled in our parts. We don't have hatred as part of our genetic code. In the war, everybody committed crimes. Croatian forests were cut down in order to build Amsterdam, and the money did not flow into Croatian treasury. It flew elsewhere. All Croatian Dalmatian forests were cut down, but nothing was built from the proceeds of the sale of timber. No theatres, no libraries, no houses for the people, and that is the main problem. Nationalism is a social phenomenon of fear before extinction. People are afraid that they would be killed. At any moment when we were sure that people would not kill us or steal from us, non-nationalism emerged in Croatia. It only emerged as a result of fear, as a result of illness, and it was only in those moments that they would make an incursion into those states and those developments that later on led to some of the deeds that were done by their political leaders of which we should certainly be ashamed. Next slide, please. Based on those facts and the aspirations of Croatian people to finally create their state, it was an aspiration, a desire, an intention, we or our ancestors entered a Nazi fascist concept, and with the assistance of Berlin and German Nazis, we created an independent State of Croatia. This is a problem which is always difficult to understand in history; namely, how come aspirations, how come desires, once they're crystallised can lead to such disorders? This is a famous question that is put; namely, that all intentions, even good ones, if implemented badly, lead straight to hell. The Independent State of Croatia stretched throughout a rather large territory, but once again it did not cover Istria, it did not include Zadar and the islands. Yes. That's what we need. In the upper portion we see that the Independent State of Croatia led by Pavelic was split into two portions. The upper portion was ruled by Germans, and the lower one was ruled by Italians. It should be noted that the army, Ustashas, which was more or less a political army of the Independent State of Croatia, was not allowed to cross into the part ruled by Italians. There it was mostly the Chetniks led by Djujic who committed plunder, murders, and so on. Those same Chetniks who some historians keep trying to include into the anti-fascist coalition. Unfortunately, this Independent State of Croatia passed certain laws. Very serious crimes were committed. Italian and German formations were dominant at the time. Italy expelled a lot of Croats from the annexed territory of Croatia. A special Italian court, between 1941 and 1943, prosecuted over 5.000 people, 500 of whom were sentenced to death. Italians also established a large number of camps, and in the Italian zone Chetniks slit the throats of over 45.000 Croats and Muslim civilians. Your Honours, we saw evidence supporting all of this, and this evidence has been translated and will be provided during the trial. Can we see the map, please -- rather, the chart. The map and the chart. On this chart, we can see the locations where camps and executions sites were located, in the lower portion. We can see Rab, Molat, Vodice, Murter, Olib, Zlarin, Lovra [phoen] and Prevlaka. All of these locations were Italian camps, and you can see how many people were killed in them. The Camps ran by Croatian political leaders were located in Jasenovac, Stara Gradiska, Gospic, Pag, and so on. All of this is painful, morbid. Too many people were killed, laid down their lives there, and all of this is a consequence of the events taking place previously in this territory which turned people into insane individuals without legal, political orientation. Those were broken-down people, broken-down individuals, desperate creatures who, under the circumstances, naturally committed serious, grave errors. In Croatia there is not a single person who today is not ashamed of such events. Following that, we have Nedic's Serbia. We can skip over that, and we get to the area under the Partisan control. Further on, please. Prior to that you saw the map of Nedic's Serbia which was a pro-fascist organisation and was among the first to subscribe to the Third Reich. And then following that you see the map entitled "Area Under Partisan Control." You see that it is split into two parts. The lower portion is under control of Italian, the upper under control of Germans, and the area in blue was controlled by Partisan formations. The Croat people in the Second World War split into two parts. Some of them joined the Independent State of Croatia and its army, the Pavelic army. However, a great number of Croats, especially in Dalmatia and northern Croatia, were among the first, among the first people in the world to join the Partisan movement. They established the first Partisan anti-fascist detachment in Europe. It was in Sisak. And out of five corps, which at the end of the war fought in the territory of Yugoslavia, three were under the command of the Supreme Staff of Croatian Partisan detachments. The suffering of the people continued. Fortunately, anti-fascism brought two things to Croatian people; rights to existence and, at the anti-fascist Assembly in AVNOJ, we were given a chance to participate in creation of Yugoslavia. On the other hand, the Communist radical minds, which do not differ greatly from Nazi and fascist minds, wanted to take revenge. So after 1945, as victors, they ceased being anti-fascists and became purely communists in the fashion of Stalin, which means that in Bleiburg and on the way of the cross they killed over 200.000 Croats. They change the ownership system, they introduced agrarian reform, and then after the conflict with Stalin, Tito imprisoned about 20.000 of his supporters and non-supporters so that one fascist state was succeeded by another fascist communist state which its brotherhood and unity system, its lack of democracy advanced through political oppression, secret services, murders, imprisonment, political trials, and so on. The economic crisis, which erupted in 1965 when hunger knocked on the doors of Yugoslavia, was resolved by opening up borders. Tito sold over 1 million individuals to the Western countries who needed workers. Unfortunately, he had these souls, and as Max Frisch, a Swiss writer said, "We looked for labourers and we got people." The problem of these two categories is a very serious, a very grave one and burdens Europe nowadays greatly. On the way of the cross, over 200.000 Croats were killed. Only in Bosnia-Herzegovina the authorities killed 5.900 persons. They convicted 341 priests and over 5.000 people. In the conflict with Stalin, 55.663 persons suffered because they were suspected of cooperating with common form. 16.000 people were imprisoned. Over a half a million people were affected. Italians were expelled from the country, thrown into pits. Polish population, Polish national minority was also expelled from Yugoslavia, and this was a very sad moment in history. It was also a war, a type of war, but a low-intensity one. Starting in 1945, over half a million of people were expelled. Italian national minority was expelled from Yugoslavia. In Goli Otok camp over 20.000 people were imprisoned, whereas in Croatia from 1945 to 1989, over 30.000 political trials were held. Among Croatian immigration, 77 persons were killed, and there were 24 unsuccessful life attempts. This was a dictatorship in the sole and legal meaning of that term. Unfortunately, when a dictator lives for a long time, such as the case with Castro, more or less people get used to the situation as it is. And then in intellectual circles certain positive phenomena emerge. The fact that people flee in boats is forgotten. Unfortunately, at the funeral of this dictator, this dictator who is among the ten greatest criminals in history of civilisation, the civilised Western world sent 120 statesmen to his funeral. The information coming from inside was very minimal. There was no interest in what was actually going on. All of this was enveloped in the so-called political interests, and our moral values, our intellectual attempts to understand things weaken every day. We get used to the situation to a greater degree. But if we're sitting somewhere drinking good wine, if we're observing French Imperialists, then everything happening around us seems to interest us less and less. Now we are switching to the table, 1945, 1980. 1980, 1989. From 1980 to 1989, we had Tito's death, the crisis in Kosovo, the intervention of JNA and police. The Congress of the League of Communists was disintegrating because a fascist creation was disintegrating. Serb intellectuals wrote the Memorandum of Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1986. Their political programme, from Moljevic, from Karadzic, Garasanin is something that they continued, considering that every piece of territory inhabited by Serbs is a Serbian piece of territory. On the 8th session, in 1987, Slobodan Milosevic became the boss of Serbia. Serbian attack on Kosovo was a devastating one. The prisons were full of Albanians, including the prisons in Croatia. The constitution of the SFRY was annulled, the autonomous regions voided, and this is how we were entering the new phase. All of the positions had been taken, catastrophe was being prepared. Everybody saw it but refused to see it. Next slide, please. The crisis in Kosovo. The intervention by the JNA and members of SUP coming from all the republics, this is quenched in blood. The miners are on strike, and all this ends up in a bad way. And now I'm going to show you the picture of the Serbian political thought vis-a-vis the area of the former Yugoslavia from Nacertanije and Gracanin. The title of the book is "Serbs Everywhere" and it is by Vuk Stefanovic, Karadzic, Moljevic, and others. Let us please just read this. Can we move on to the next slide, please. This is a map, and it is self-explanatory. In all the Serbian intellectual and political documents, this is exactly what they show as their desire. And let's move on to the next one. The Memorandum of the Serbian Academy, dating from 1986, which is based on the same thoughts. This is the translation. I would kindly ask the gentlemen to read. And this is a long text. Can we move on, please. The constitution of Yugoslavia was annulled. And if we move on, we will see how Yugoslavia was being conquered. There were rallies of people. There was shouting. Kosovo was conquered. The constitution of Yugoslavia was annulled. The autonomous provinces, which had had their own constitutions, now were brought under the control of Serbia, and they ceased existing as integral parts of Yugoslavia. Between 1889 [as interpreted] and 1990, on the 1st of September at the 14th Congress, Yugoslavia was completely dissolved. Yugoslavia could no longer exist. Parties were formed in Croatia. There were elections in Croatia in April and in May of 1990, and people over there elected their representatives in a very peaceful atmosphere. They exercised their free will, and Dr. Franjo Tudjman became not just the president of Croatia, actually he became the president of the Presidency. So, Mr. Scott, would you please correct this imprecision in your thoughts. And first -- before that, I would like to say that the system of Yugoslavia had two main components. One component was the Yugoslav People's Army, and the second component was the Territorial Defence. And this was a defence system of the former Yugoslavia. The Territorial Defence was linked to the republics, and it was managed and governed by the republican authorities. This was within the framework of the strategy of All People's Defence. When they realised that a strike on Yugoslavia came from east or from west, from the NATO alliance, as the then power wielders thought, the army would not be able to sustain such strikes, and it was expected from the armed people to take over the defence, because nobody was allowed to sign capitulation. Every company, therefore, every institution had in its storerooms the weapons that they had bought with their own money and that they would use for their own defence. In 1990, the Yugoslav People's Army forcibly, without any questions asked and without the right to do so, alleviated from Croatia and from Bosnia-Herzegovina all of the weapons of the Territorial Defence. They stole it from these two republics. Nothing remained. And thus the people were left bare-handed to fight against the force in strength -- military force in Europe that would soon show its ugly face and its bestiality. The strike against Croatia happened on the 17th of August, 1990. On the map you can see that there was a rebellion, and the regular police station was taken. And when the helicopters of the Croatian police wanted to quench the rebellion, when they wanted to send their police officers to prevent the strike against the constitutional order of the state, they were intercepted by the aircraft of the JNA. They forced them to land at the Bihac airport, and that day can be considered the beginning of war in Croatia. Because if somebody uses military force to prevent you from exercising your constitutional rights, then this can be considered aggression, and this is therefore the date when war is considered to start in a state. Thirty-five years ago, as a young student, I bought a book by Werner Heisenberg, a Nobel Prize winner, a physicist, who is an authority in quantum mechanics. The name of the book is "Teil Und Ganz." In that book, which is full of valuable discussions on the theory of motion, and especially in the discussions between the Newton's and Einstein's principles of mechanical causal link that cannot be replaced by any other link and the new science of quantum mechanics which was more based on statistics and is considered to be a statistical variant and distribution of what can bring us closer to the truth and which can be applied to any notion, including the notions at this Tribunal which is whether it is possible to establish direct and clear as well as firm links between the phenomenology of war and those who participated in the war, such as Mr. Scott wants us to understand, those are differential quotations that belong to society. They're non-linear, they're statistical. They're equations which change day in, day out in the turbulences that are not easy to solve. There are not final solutions to these equations, and we have to start from scratch. And when we do that, we end up with two bad solutions. Under such circumstances, there is usually no good solution, and very often you are between a rock and a hard place and you have to choose between the two evils, the one that will end up in less adverse consequences. And this is the main problem. But let's not dwell upon physics. Let me say that in 1933, young Heisenberg was desperate because prosecutions started in Germany. Jews were being expelled from universities, books were torched, and he went to see his older colleague, Professor Planck, also a Nobel Prize winner, a big name, the author of "Planck's Constant Equation," and I'm going to read just one thing that he told him. "You came here to ask me for advice on political issues." This is what Planck said. "But I'm afraid I can't give you any advice. I do not have any hope that the catastrophe that threatens Germany and German universities can still be stopped in any way. Nobody can impact the avalanche that has started moving. And what this avalanche is going to destroy, how many human lives it is going to take, it is the natural laws that have already decided that, although we still don't know it." And I underline the word "natural laws." "The energy of a society at certain moments are natural laws. Hatred, desperation, pain, expulsion, death, a lost hope, lost morale, lost expectations for things from international -- from the international community. Those are all natural laws. And in that whirlwind, the way an individual is going to act is very hard to predict." Then he continues to say: "If you don't resign, if you stay here, your task will be a very different one. You cannot stop this catastrophe. In order to survive, you have to constantly engage in compromise, but you can, you can try, together with others, to create the islands of survival. I believe that all those who can do something, that all those who are able to do something and are not forced to move out because their race does not compel them to do so, they should stay here and prepare the future. This is going to be very difficult, and it is going to be tied with danger. The compromises that you will have to do will be held against you in the future. Maybe you will be punished for them. However, maybe you have to do that. Of course, I cannot hold it against anybody who decides differently. If they -- they don't find the life in Germany worth living, if they cannot support the injustices being done in Germany, that they cannot prevent any of these injustices happening when they decide to leave. However, under such terrible circumstances as prevail today in Germany, one cannot act justly. One cannot act as they should. And irrespective of the decision that you might take, you will be a participant in some sort of justice. Whatever your decision may be, you will be a participant in justice. So at the end of the day, everybody has to look at themselves. It is pointless for anybody to either give or receive advice. Therefore, I can tell you don't hope that anything you might do until the end of the catastrophe may prevent some of the disasters. However, when you take your decision, think of the time that -- that are ahead of us." Ten thousands wars have been recorded in the history of humankind, and an intellectual is always faced with the dilemma whether to escape, whether to flee, or whether to stay. What will be his power of action if he stay? But this is not the matter of his own will or desire but of strength. We did not create evil. We struggled against it. If you struggle, that doesn't mean that you're going to succeed, that you are going to prevail. However, we're going to prove here -- I'm going to prove here, using clear evidence, that day in, day out, we had to make 50 or 60 decision a day, that we had people who were killed, who were injured, who were expelled, that our country had been attacked, that an aggression was undertaken against it. It was not a state. It was being created as a state. It changed its political system and all the while it suffered aggression. This is what I'm going to prove with clear evidence. In 1991, some things happened, as you can see them in this slide. And on the map you're going to see the Serbian aggression against Croatia. Pakrac, beginning of March, 1991. Plitvice on the 31st of March, 1991. Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991. The Yugoslav People's Army attacked Slovenia. The war was very short because Slovenia was not part of the political plans of Serbia to ever become part of Serbia. Again, a map of the general aggression of Serbia, Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina against Croatia. Now, I have to tell you one thing: If Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state in formal and legal terms, then it was an aggressor against Croatia. From the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia was attacked. Throughout the war, Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a formal and legal entity, if this is how we're going to consider it, was an aggressor against Croatia with huge consequences. Two-thirds of the borders near Dubrovnik, near Dalmatia, near Sisak, near Vukovar, at those places Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked Croatia. Of course the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had been conquered by Serbia. But this today is a state with legal and political continuity. And when stock is going to be taken who owes who and who was aggressor against whom, then Bosnia and Herzegovina has to be considered an aggressor against Croatia. Of course there were attempts to disarm the police. There was a referendum on independence. Here you see the Brioni Declaration. Once that Croatia declared its independence, once its parliament declared Croatia's independence, the Brioni Declaration happened on the 7th of July, 1991. It was demanded from the Croatian president and the Croatian parliament to delay the declaration of Croatian independence by three months. The European Union and the Western states wanted this to be frozen, an application of such a decision, in order to give an opportunity to the negotiators to find a solution over the period of three months, a solution that would not lead to a war. And according to a good old custom, Croatia accepted that. There was no reason not to accept that. On the 7th of July, this is what happened. Three months later, on the last day of this moratorium on the decision on the proclamation of the independence, Serbian army, the Yugoslav People's Army, shelled the seat of the government in Zagreb, Banski Dvori. At that moment, Ante Markovic, the president of the federal government, and Dr. Franjo Tudjman, the president of the Presidency of the Croatian state, were sitting in that building. Can we see the slide, please. Yes. Leave it there. Three months after this, on the last day, they tried to kill Franjo Tudjman, because the number of agents of the military counter-intelligence service and the secret service of the interior in Croatia was such that they knew where everybody was eating, sleeping, where they moved. But fortunately, one minute before the bombing - and you will see a video of it later - Franjo Tudjman left the room. This was a terrorist action par excellence. In September and November 1992, in Slavonski Brod and the surrounding area 182 persons were killed by shelling and bombing from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were shelling the town. They were killing the town. I ask, did Alija Izetbegovic ever state his position on this? No. Did he offer Franjo Tudjman a military agreement on common defence? No. If there is no military agreement between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, then according to the constitution of Croatia, a Croatian soldier, even under orders, must not cross over to the other side. And the Croatian soldiers who are said to have participated in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina could not have been issued the order to cross over into the neighbouring territory. They could only have gone of their own accord. Twenty-seven children were killed. Let us see the slide showing these children. Please let's see the slide. This is what created and gave rise to the energy of society, to the emotional tension. It is pictures like these, pictures from Vukovar, pictures from Zadar, pictures from Dubrovnik; imagines of those who had been expelled or killed. These are the images the Croatian people were living with. This is the war as experienced by the Croatian people. And this is what one has to bear in mind when one considers the decisions and the speeches made by a particular politician in a particular time and place. I was a volunteer in the Posavina area. And even if I had illegally issued an order to someone to go there, he could have refused without any consequences or punishment. Let everybody show me a single Croatian soldier who was punished because he rejected an illegitimate order to cross over to the other side, then we can discuss that. There were those who made use of their right, but it was never legally established that they should go there. Your Honours, if you think it's time for a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. It is now 3.30. We're going to have a technical break of 20 minutes, and we shall resume around ten to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, learned gentlemen, a correction. At the beginning, I was told that I mispronounced a word. I said French Imperialists. I meant to refer to the French impressionists. This was a slip on my part. So I wish to introduce the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. In the next portion, we shall see some opinions about the beginning of the solution of the crisis and the various standpoints expressed in the international community in various Arbitration Commissions and other bodies about the beginning of the crisis and how it could be solved. For example, the Arbitration Commission was of the opinion that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is now in the process of its disintegration. Next, please. The parliament of the Republic of Croatia issued a declaration about the aggression against the Republic of Croatia. Next, please. Next, please. Next, please. The parliament of the Republic of Croatia reached a decision on the 8th of October, 1991, about severing links. Then the peace conference in Yugoslavia. The opinion of the Arbitration Commission. Next, please. What is the Croatian response? First of all, Croatia formed a large number of peace movements such as the Mother's for Peace. The Croatian Art Forces. These were groups of artists trying to show in every possible way that it is the wish of the Croatian people and it's legally elected leadership to have only a peaceful and dignified separation from the other republics and states, which were, under the constitution, states in the former federation of Yugoslavia. Then there was the Brioni Declaration. Then there was the Sarajevo truce. Next slide, please. The parliament of the Republic of Croatia issued a new conclusion. The same things were constantly repeated. That is, that Croatia would be a democratic state with the highest standards of protection of minority rights known in the European Community. All of these documents are collected in a book. There are 227 of them. Everything that was signed by any institution of the Croatian state, including the president of the state, the parliament, the cabinet. Nowhere ever was a document signed or a word spoken in public or an agreement entered into bringing into question the integrity, the territorial integrity of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There are 227 documents. These are letters, decisions, peace conferences and so on. Never did any legally elected body of the Croatian state bring into question the survival, existence and territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Had -- or, rather, the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina had a problem with its internal organisation because it is inhabited by three sovereign and constituent peoples, and like every sovereign people, each one of these peoples has the right to question the internal organisation of the state and see what rights both as a nation and as individual citizens they will have within that state, this was the basic and only problem and the cause of all the misfortunes after Serbia committed an aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, setting in motion an unprecedented avalanche of hatred, suffering, and pain. In the Lisbon Declaration on Yugoslavia, issued by the ministers of foreign affairs of the European Community of the 17th of February, 1992, it says that the conference supports dialogue, the dialogue of all interested parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with a view to a constitutional solution which will have to take into account the legitimate aspirations of all the peoples within the inviolate borders of that republic. The Cutileiro Plan of the 9th of March, 1992, which was the basis for the question posed at the referendum within the framework of the Badinter Commission, which was to issue a legal opinion on whether and how the republics could become states, the following is stated: "Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a state comprising a certain number of constituent units based on national foundations and taking into account the economic, geographic and other criteria. Sovereignty resides in citizens of the Muslim, Croatian, and Serbian peoples and members of other peoples and groups who exercised a sovereignty within the constituent units and organs of the republic. Within the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, constituent units will be established, the territory of which is defined in part E of this text." Therefore, the idea of national interests and the territorial framework of these national interests was not purely the idea of the Croatian leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was, on the contrary, the standpoint of the international community before the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Cutileiro Plan of the 18th of March, 1992, provided for Bosnia and Herzegovina being a state made up of three constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographic, and other criteria. All these documents are contained in this collection of 227 documents in the form of a book. And I will repeat once again that nowhere and never did the institutions of the Republic of Croatia bring into question or challenge the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Please, let's move on. Yugoslavia in 1985, this is the disposition of the armies of the JNA. This is how the JNA territorially divided Yugoslavia. This is a military arrangement. In 1987, as preparation for the aggression against Croatia, there was a reorganisation of the JNA. The JNA established a new territorial division, and as you can see, it corresponds to the notorious Serbian political plan that everything from the Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag line should belong to Serbia. This military district with its command in Belgrade was drawn up as the future implementation of political plans. This is how the war was to unfold, not as isolated events here and there in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. This war cannot be seen in bits and pieces of that kind. It was an integral war in which two-thirds of Croatia and all of Bosnia and Herzegovina were in line with everything that we have heard about before in Serbian political thought were to become part of Serbia. Let's move on. The operative deployment of forces, they moved some corps towards Serbia. Others they moved towards Bihac. The 13th was moved from Pula to Montenegro, and there was preparations were already underway for an all-out attack on the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could we have the next slide, please. The national structure of the officers in the army is shown here. It does not correspond by any means to the ethnic make-up of Yugoslavia. Here we can see what the difference is. There are 51 per cent more Serbs in relation to the overall population, 148 per cent more Montenegrins, whereas 5.3 less Croats, 6.6 less Slovenes, 7.8 less Muslims, and so on. There are fewer Albanians and more Yugoslavs. Let's move on. Please, next slide. Unfortunately, we now come to the painful portion of this story, and that is the question: Who was actually truly capable of preventing the war in Yugoslavia? Who had the information about what was going on? I knew it, but my power was not such as to stop a war. When Mr. Baker stated in Belgrade that it was the wish of the United States for Yugoslavia to continue in existence, then it was considered a legitimate right of the Secretary of State of the United States to express political will and desire of its government. However, gentlemen, given everything that was going on prior to that, given what had been prepared, what were the real implications of such words? Somebody has a right to put a red sweater on somebody. However, if you put a red sweater on somebody who is in the middle of a bullfight with nine wild bulls, then the consequences are more than clear. Unfortunately, this is what happened in this situation, whether we recognise it or not, whether it's hard for us to accept it or not. But the facts imply this. Here is green light. Go on. You have no weapons, not even the ones you purchased with your own funds. We want the state to continue in existence, and you have to find the ways. I don't think that Mr. Baker or any of those who supported the continued existence of the state were aware of the implications, were aware of what was going to happen. However, the Serbs interpreted these words in such a way. Therefore, ignorance, unfortunately, led to events that are known to everyone. The next event which borders on any possible and rational understanding is the declaration -- or, rather, Resolution 713 of the Security Council, which introduced embargo on weapons import. As far as I'm aware, all Resolutions of the United Nations speak and confirm the unlimited right of all peoples to defence of their nations. If you leave all peoples without weapons except for Serbs and the war is about to begin or has even begun, what can one expect? What else can you explain other than a massacre inflicted by mad army. This Resolution, this barbarian Resolution would be annulled too late. Later on, they would look elsewhere, turn their head another way. They would allow our ships to pass. They would do, yes, but I think that this Resolution is contrary to any elementary, ethical values. This Resolution is something that I'm unable to explain. And if that is the case, then these important international institutions do not impress me at all. Next slide, please. On the 20th of March, 1992, the JNA deployed its forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. These forces were ready. Everything was prepared, and the aggression rushed ahead full speed. You see all the marks indicating what formations were deployed where, how many soldiers, how many tanks. Next slide, please. This slide shows how many volunteers, how many soldiers were at the disposal of this army. We can't go into too many details here. Let us continue. There is a continuous story here about the meeting between President Tudjman and Milosevic in Karadjordjevo. Nobody else was present, however everybody else knows what was discussed there. If you look at the map, if you look at the imperial aspirations of Serbia, then the logical question is this: How was Franjo Tudjman able to discuss with Milosevic the division of Bosnia when Croatia, under his plans, had no border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, because Bosnia and Herzegovina did not exist? So what were they able to discuss then? This goes contrary to any rational logic. This story was invented. It was invented later on within later interpretations of guilt, of shutting your eyes before facts and airing dirty laundry, because steps were not done, steps that civilisation expected them to do. It was possible to stop the war, to prevent the war had they so wanted. They had the power. They had the abilities. They should have put UN peacekeeping forces along borders. They should have used force to make it impossible for things to happen as they did. They should have forced these republics to opt for democracy, which is something that Croatia had already done. They should have forced them to abide by all fundamental human rights. Had they done this, there would have been no victims, no numerous victims. This is a letter sent by -- by President Izetbegovic to President Tudjman speaking about the friendship and friendly sentiments between Croatian and Muslim people and saying, "Do not enter into any agreements with him," meaning Milosevic. Further on, we see the Geneva agreement on the pull-out of the JNA from Croatia. Once again, a situation that has no sense. Most of Croatian territory had already been occupied at this point. There was an aggression against Vukovar. Many cities were devastated. 250.000 people were deported. And what we refer to as the international community forces Franjo Tudjman and the Croatian government to use the weapons of the JNA in the JNA depots in Croatia and to transport it to Bosnia and Herzegovina as though, for God's sake, they had no idea what was going to happen. They had no idea, even though there were previous examples. Naturally, this only filled up the depots of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina and led to all the consequences that shock our conscience. And it is very difficult under the circumstances to pinpoint the guilt. It is especially difficult to establish what right one has to give political speeches and who is responsible for consequences of those speeches. Now we have to look at the political climate among Bosnians as it existed before the conflict erupted. Can we see the Islamic Declaration, please. Can we see the political platform, please. We have the Islamic Declaration and then the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Assembly session was interrupted. People started praying. Then there was a referendum, and so on. This is what Bosnia and Herzegovina looked like. You have the number of inhabitants; so many Muslims, so many Serbs, so many Croats and others, and so on. The next slide, please. Alija Izetbegovic served a nine-year prison sentence as an Islamic fundamentalist in the prison in Yugoslavia, and this is where he wrote his Islamic project known as Islamic Declaration. We translated certain bits of it and I would appeal to Their Honours and everybody else to read them. Further on, please. Two important things: First, prior to first elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this book was published in 200.000 copies as a political blueprint that had to be implemented. There are two essential parts here. Islamic individuals and non-Islamic cannot live together. And if one -- once there are more than 50 per cent of us, we will introduce Islamic laws into Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a man who wrote this in prison, who published it in 200.000 copies. Once this is read by other nations, then it is clear that we cannot agree with this. This causes us to have concerns, fear, and not understand this. It causes us to differ in opinion and to come to different results. Even though initially these differences did not seem to be so great, later on applying the laws of the theory of chaos, once events are reiterated and once they escalate, these differences grow. They grow in size. And at one point in time, without anybody noticing it, we reach what is known as a singular point and everything before us explodes into complete chaos, which is practically beyond control. Next slide, please. Referendum, please. Now we reach the issue of referendum. How is it possible to simultaneously defend the thesis saying that Croatia wants to annex a portion of Bosnian territory, and then at the same time have Croatian people go out to referendum to vote, which was a precondition for the Badinter Commission to give green light to European Community to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state. So first of all, let us recognise them, and then later on the rest can be done. This can be done either by idiots or by fools, or this does not fit with the thesis that there is anybody in Croatian leadership who wants to confiscate Bosnian territory. Referendum was the place, was the mechanism for that. Failure to vote in the referendum meant that they could not get 51 per cent of the votes, because Serbs did not want to participate in the referendum. So there was no way for Bosnia to become an independent state. I can tell you this: The grave fate of Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina over the centuries did not create among this nation a sentiment that Bosnia and Herzegovina was their homeland. No. They were forced to live there. The borders were drawn under fire, under the range of Turkish cannons. People were separated by force. This was not the state that could have created among its inhabitants a sense of homeland. Political mentality and pragmatism of Franjo Tudjman was such that he suggested by all possible means to Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina to go to the referendum and to vote for independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is why, gentlemen from the Prosecution, the response was far greater on the second day than the first day, because this was an appeal issued by the people. The people cannot be ordered but appeals can be issued to them. Invitations and calls can be issued to them. And this is precisely the reason why the Croat inhabitants in Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the referendum and stated that they considered Bosnia and Herzegovina to be a state. Can we see the film, please. We're now about to see what the conduct of Croatian citizens in Bosnia and Herzegovina was, as well as in Herzegovina, at the moment when the tanks of Yugoslav People's Army were headed towards Kupresko Polje in order to carry out an attack on Split. We will see what their conduct was. We will see what they said, what they did, and how they greeted Alija Izetbegovic in this entire story, because they had already seen what the tanks meant and what they would do once they're allowed in. They knew that this significantly threatened the entire southern portion of Croatia, from Split further south. Can we see the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] So they already started shooting in Mostar. Perisic started shelling, Karadzic saying. Karadzic said that there was no way for Bosnia and Herzegovina to continue existing, because Serbs would refuse living in such Bosnia-Herzegovina. Serbs have entered this state under certain preconditions that were recorded in AVNOJ, and they do not recognise republic borders as future state borders. So throughout Yugoslavia, republic borders were legitimate and were in place. Milosevic says that the compromise solution on federation is unacceptable. By applying the confederation formula, Yugoslavia would disintegrate, and he doesn't want to accept that. This is why we cannot accept that nor we intend to do so. And this is Alija Izetbegovic responding to him on his -- on his behalf and on behalf of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Mr. Izetbegovic saying: "They're announcing an even bloodier war. Our duty, duty of us, citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would be to prevent at any cost this bloodshed. However, as you can see not only are we unable to, people much more powerful than us are unable to do that. What we can do is to refuse to participate in it. Thus starting from the sovereignty of the republics, starting from the position of the Presidency by accurately interpreting the will of the majority of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I hereby declare neutrality of Bosnia and Herzegovina at this point in time. Unfortunately, today we live in a time where one needs more courage to participate in peace than to participate in war. I plead with you to summon up enough courage and to refuse to participate in this war. This is not our war." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Isn't this wonderful to listen to somebody saying they want neutrality. However, at this point in time Croatians in Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been killed, expelled. There was no more neutrality any more. At this point in time when Mr. Izetbegovic speaks of neutrality, he has in mind only Muslims. We Croats do not have neutrality any more. We are threatened. Our existence is threatened. Mr. Izetbegovic said that this was not our war, and this did not refer to us Croats. Everything was already on fire. His people were being killed in Bijeljina and he says this is not our war. He had already seen that on the territory of the state whose legal president he is, so many children have been killed, so many troops sent to war with Croatia, so that this neutrality is nothing but a platitude. Before that - and we are going to show it now - in two places there was aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina; the village of Unista near Knin, and the village of Ravno. Can we see the video clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] First we're going to see the tanks in Prolog where they were stopped by the people there themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The army has to withdraw, but they are not withdrawing. Behind Listica the column starts. Hundreds of vehicles, cars, lorries blocking the road all the way to Prolog. When they return, we go back." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We want peace.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The generals want us to defend ourselves. The citizens doubt the good intentions of the army. When asked why they stopped the column, they say, we have a counter-question: Why here? Why the army? The soldier repeats, We are going to Duvno field for regular exercise. The people don't want conflict. They're against it. In the course of the night, we had very good behaviour and no incidents. It's very difficult to estimate the number of people who have gathered here, but their request is what they have in common. From here the army cannot proceed. We want peace." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] They're singing about love and peace.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] For three days in a row the army and the people are at a stalemate. That is why around 1300 hours Izetbegovic, Tuleban [phoen], Pelivan and Kljuic arrived here, trying to convince the people to let the army go. "You have to trust me because I can't betray you. Even if I wanted to betray you, I spent nine years in prison as a young man and three years as an adult, and I have never betrayed anybody." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] This is how the Croatian people greeted the tanks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Thank you very much. Thank you very much. What I'm saying is I can make a mistake, but as a human being I believe that you should let the column go. However, they don't agree for the tank column to go towards Croatia." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] This is a story about Mr. Izetbegovic having been captured by the JNA at the airport near Sarajevo. The president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was arrested by General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. Izetbegovic, the army can transport you to Sarajevo, can't they? "Izetbegovic: Yes, they might, but they said that they will be attacked. General Djordjevic issued an order to cease fire. He's ordering everybody to cease fire. "Can we speak to the general, Mr. President? Our request is that this --" THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] This is General Djordjevic speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] -- we want the attacks to stop on our barracks. Secondly, we want our injured to be transported. Thirdly, we -- we have other requests. We are not going to -- towards Sarajevo. We are going towards Lukavica. Mr. Izetbegovic, who is a sensible man, who is here with his daughter in Lagumdzija, is safe. Here, in 15 minutes, he will receive medical care. He will be comfortable, and he will lack nothing. "General Djordjevic, you are a soldier. What is the status of Mr. President in your barracks? "He is a person who has to help the army to save lives. I hope you are not going to blackmail us by having captured the president. Call General Kukanjac and you will be clear on everything. There's no fire from Lukavica. Lukavica is under fire. In the hall where I am, there are 50 people, half of them from abroad. "Yes, fire is being opened from here, and I am afraid that a third party has gotten involved, the party that wants a conflict to break out between the citizens and the JNA. I believe that those are our paramilitaries from the SDS which are opening fire from Mount Trebevic. They're opening fire on the army. "The TO will cease fire, and after that, we will try and get our soldiers out of the encirclement. Doyle will come and pick you up. Ask the TO to cease fire. "Ganic, you have my full authority to issue orders until I find myself again in the Presidency building. Your orders are my orders too." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: Stop. I would like to comment upon the first clip as well as on the second clip. Do these people that saw in the clip really want a war? Did they display any hatred when they distributed chocolate among the others? And the second comment: The president of Presidency was captured by the JNA but everybody missed one of the fundamental legal issues that can be seen here. Izetbegovic, at the end, says: "Ganic, if I don't come back, you take over and issue orders." Ganic is not the one who should have issued orders instead of him, according to the constitution. It should have been Stjepan Kljuic, a Croat. When the president of a state skips the constitutional procedure and leaves his fellow national, a Muslim, the right to rule and not his rightful successor, Stjepan Kljuic, then this can be considered a pustch in the legal practice. Of course everybody saw that, those who wanted to see that. Later on, this was ignored, this was forgotten because it did not suit anybody. Of course, after having suffered greatly, the Muslims found themselves in the position in which many of the things that they did in a very bad way at the detriment of the Croats were finally forgotten. Not only did Bosnia and Herzegovina launch aggression against Croatia, but also the Muslims in Central Bosnia when they realised that they could not defeat the Serbs, they turned their weapons against the HVO. Let's now move on. Let me just tell you before that, he's going to talk about hatred. Maybe we can fast forward to that bit when he speaks about hatred. Hatred and weapons. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Unlawfulness or stupid laws that were inherited from the Bolshevik state. Only naive people can buy that game, that game which is played. And somebody is saying this is no longer the Yugoslav People's Army, this is the Serbian army, but Belgrade has nothing whatsoever to do with it. In our view, the JNA, Belgrade, and Serbia are all responsible for what is being done in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "The intention of all this was military cooperation in order to prevent aggression. As you know, this was a simultaneous aggression, first against Croatia and then against Bosnia-Herzegovina, and currently what is under way is aggression against ..." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] A few months before this was not his war. At the Split agreement, again he was against it. I participated in that. We asked for a military alliance that would have enabled us to work together. We ended up with a contract which did not allow Croatia to participate fully in the creation of joint forces that would counter the aggression. Can we now move on to the Patriotic League, please. On the 17th of April, 1991, before the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established, the Serbs ceded, separated themselves from all the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They said that this was not their state, that they would not agree to what the others wanted, and they launched the entire aggression. The Muslim and Bosniak response to all that was to establish the so-called Patriotic League. The Patriotic League was established on the 17th of April, and it was made up of Muslims only. Its pledge read as follows: "I swear by the Allah Jelleshsnuhu that I shall at all times and in all places defend the interests of the Muslim people." Nobody else was mentioned here. The Patriotic League was established by the creme de la creme of the Muslim people. It is based on the Islamic Declaration. It doesn't mention the multi-ethnic state of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina where all people would be equal. Obviously -- can we move on, please. The order of the Main Staff of the Patriotic League reads: "Our forces are organised into the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina in formations ranging from a platoon to the brigade, with the strengths of 120.000 people. When the fighting starts, we will probably get more people." These are the foundations of the Patriotic League. The president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina Hasan Cengic, one of the key people, Sulejman Vranj, at the same time, simultaneously, they want to advocate the totality of all the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but at the same time, before Herceg-Bosna, before any establishment of the Croatian people that had already seen, was ready and knew what to expect from the Serbs because they had seen in it in Vukovar and elsewhere. This is where the difference is and the foundation of the politics rise from. Now I'm showing you a document written by Mr. Izetbegovic. This is a decision appointing commanders of all the units of the Territorial Defence. On the 27th of May, 1992, the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina is in full range, full reign. And he also appointed 39 commanders. Can we see the table, please. Among the 39 appointed commanders of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are 43 Muslims, accounting for 97.73 per cent. There is only one Serb, and there are no Croats at all. Don't you think that these are all starting points that will only widen the gap despite the efforts to reconciliate things? There's not a single Croat here. It was only then that the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was issued in response to what the Serbs had started and the Muslims finished by establishing the Patriotic League. Nobody with any responsibility for his own people within the framework of the existing constitution and rights arising from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia about the right to association that applied not only to municipalities but also to the association of municipalities when it came to defending one's own life, the life of their families, I remind you that on the 10th of April, 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina stopped existing at any level. There was no electricity. There was no government. There was no police. There was no banks, no bread, no shops, no communication. There was no money, nothing. There was no currency. People were left to their own means. When you have something that we call zero civilisation level, you start creating the so-called embryos, and this is where we encounter one of the fundamental problems of understanding, when we here use the words "government," "army," "general," when we use the words "the Ministry of Justice," then we imply contents that are valid and can be applied in France or the United States of America. You do not take into account the fact that this is just a piece of paper that have proclaimed themselves a government. They did not have a car. They did not have a telephone. These 15 people were just groups of people who were controlling other groups of people who were afraid and those who had seen on television what had happened to their co-nationals in Croatia. This is not government, this is not the army. This is not the Ministry of Justice as we know it. It was only in 1993 in the month of March that the minister of justice got a telephone line in his office. You can desire things, but whether you can do them is a different thing. There a lot of effort was invested in making this embryo grow into something, but there was chaos. Chaos reigned. The number of expelled got bigger, and their problems were so great - and I'm going to show you some data on that - that this went beyond the capabilities of much better organised states than Bosnia was at the time. And if we could say that a 40-year-old democracy is a mature democracy, then what we had after five weeks was nothing but an embryo of such democracy. Can we please go on. On the 10th of May, 1991, there was an attack from Knin after the Croatian village of Kijevo had been burnt down and the people killed. There was an attack of -- on Unista, which is on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the legal system of any state, the aggression on the territory of that state is a cause of war or a declaration of war, or at least it gives rise to a protest. But not for a single moment did the government in Sarajevo or the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, respond to this attack. Why? Because there were no Muslims there. Let's take a look at Ravno now. On the 15th of September, 1991, and the 16th of September, 1991, the village of Ravno in Bosnia and Herzegovina was razed to the ground. People were killed. After that, Mr. Izetbegovic made the statement we heard: "This is not our war." Gentlemen, it was our war. I don't know whether it was his war, but for the Croats, it was our war, and no one had the right not to do everything in their power to establish an organisation that would prevent such things from happening, or at least to offer resistance, even if it meant getting killed. Let's move on. Let's skip over that. We now have the siege of Sarajevo in April. It was then that the gentlemen in Sarajevo thought the war began. But it didn't begin then. The map of Mostar, which had been occupied by the Serb previously, and the bombing which will be presented to Your Honours through evidence, everything was destroyed, but nobody cared about this. Let's move on. This is the territory occupied by the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska in April and in November. Bosnia and Herzegovina was already occupied. Weapons were being used. Let's see how many refugees, first Muslims and then Croats, arrived from these territories either to what we call the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna -- over 30.000 refugees were looked after by this organisation referred to as the HZ HB, because it was well organised. Had it not been organised, it could not distributed food to these people or provided them with accommodation. However, 30.000 people were provided with accommodation on that small territory, among that population which was not very numerous. Let's move on. The occupied part of Eastern Mostar. Let me touch upon Mostar briefly. Zenica and the east part of Mostar were occupied. When the JNA expelled all the Muslims from the eastern part, they were all accommodated in the western part. In June 1992, I led the attack for the liberation of Mostar, and a few days later up to the right bank of the Neretva and beyond. Never did we fail to take care of anybody. Over 20.000 Muslims arrived from that side, and they were all cared for. Far more Muslims than Croats entered flats abandoned by Serbs, JNA officers. A far larger number of Muslims than Serbs moved into empty flats illegally. On the army of BH, or the Muslim side, there was only one battalion with about 150 men. The question we should ponder is how one battalion, without Croatian assistance, could grow into the 4th Corps of the BH army in half of Mostar. Everything they received, food, clothing, weapons, medicines, hospital treatment, everything they had they got from the Croats. But this was just preparation for the next conflict. After this, Travnik, Vares, and Kakanj was occupied by them. Fojnica was occupied. Jablanica, Bugojno were occupied. Konjic. All this was done by the BH army. One town after another were occupied. People were expelled, crimes were committed. Let's move on. Can we see the document on that peace conference, please. Your Honours, you have before you a document that reads as follows: "Report on the activity of the international conference on the protection of human rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Of course, as you can see, this conference was held in Zagreb, in Croatia. The criminal plan of Franjo Tudjman implies that he quite peacefully allows an international conference on the protection of human rights. In this conference, there is no one who is not a Muslim from Qatar, Jordan, Arabia, Pakistan, Malaysia, and so on and so forth. These were all leaders of Muslim states and organisations, all of them in Zagreb. After that, they went on a visit, but let's skip over all this now. We'll skip over all this for want of time. Let's skip over all this. Refugees and displaced persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let's look at the map on the table. These are the routes taken by refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina. All these routes could go in only one direction, and that was towards Croatia. They arrived in Split. Many of them remained on territory in Herzegovina which had a 90 per cent Croatian majority. And then, via Split, they went all over Croatia. And if we look at the next table -- let's skip over this and just look at the table. Can we see the routes taken by the refugees? I wish to draw your attention to the fact that pink here represents the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia, and the south-north communication was only through one ferry line. Four hundred thousand displaced persons. Twenty-one thousand arrive in the Republic of Croatia, and they were all looked after. Let's move on. Can we now see the BH plan for the conquest of Central Bosnia? We here deal with Urbicid, and all this information will be provided to Your Honours so that based on all the relevant facts and the inter-connections between those facts Your Honours may reach your own conclusions. Let's move on. This is the Neretva 93 plan. It's a plan of attack by Muslim forces on the HVO. This plan, as far as I know, has already been seen before this Tribunal. The intention was to reach not only Neum but also Ploca, which is on Croatian territory. This offensive lasted over a month and a half. After Vares was taken and looted, with the cynical thesis that we had abandoned it in order to resettle the population according to the OTP, Kakanj, Bugojno, Fojnica, Jablanica, Konjic - and we will show only parts of these - after 124.000 civilians were --

It's not the will of Slobodan Praljak or the others here as to whether it will happen but only how it can be prevented. Let's move on. Let's move on. Let's move on. Konjic. Let's move on. The Mujahedin. For every municipality you have this. These are not the final numbers. These are the minimum certain numbers, 1.124 people. Of course, the Prosecutor is right, and no one must even think that one evil can justify another. However, evil does produce evil, and I will show you some examples of how this happens everywhere in developed and civilised country. As the Nobel Laureate Planck said, these are the laws of nature, the first law of thermal dynamics; action and reaction. Unfortunately, that is how human beings are constructed. When their pain and their grief overwhelms them and becomes stronger than their morality, people lose control and do evil things. Under such conditions it is immensely difficult to keep this under control. We have hundreds of examples in Iraq and elsewhere, showing what well-organised and well-ordered army is capable of doing. In a terrible situation with a lot of understanding, when people are being killed in Sarajevo, when the international community is still imposing an embargo and yet failing to bomb Serb positions, when they are not responding, he opened the doors to the Mujahedin. They did not arrive as such. They all arrived with IDs belonging to humanitarian organisations. We had to let them through. When we stopped the first convoy that we stopped - and I participated in that - there was an outcry, and afterwards everybody was very surprised. But when someone is being killed as the Muslims were being killed in Sarajevo and elsewhere, had they been offered assistance by the devil, by Hitler, they would not have refused. When they were coming in, saying that they were there to help, of course you accepted their help. People were being killed, and they accepted their help, because later on when they put themselves under the protectorate of the international community, look what happened in Srebrenica. Yes, it was done by the Serbs, but many others are also guilty, because one had to know. One had to know what was likely to happen and what our decision would mean, but nothing was done except to wait and wait and wait. Let's look at the film. Here are their first and last names, their photographs. Let's look at the film.
