"But you have to worry also about his soldiers that are [inaudible] and it's not your attitude [inaudible]." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, let us continue further on. I wish to mention one issue here. The Chetnik gangs were singing the following there: "Slobodan -" meaning Milosevic - "send us meat -- or, rather, send us salad. There will be meat. We will be slitting throats of Croats." It was painful to hear BBC reporters say that Serbs were singing their nationalist songs. This is a painful confrontation with civilisation and ethical values. Now, the conduct of the Republic of Croatia. International community came up with Cutileiro Plan in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Vance-Owen Plan we also see various provinces. The same applies to Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, and then the Washington Agreement provided some sort of a final solution. I wish to emphasise that each document put on the table by the international community proposed to Croatia as a participant was always signed first by Croatian leadership. Both Croatian leadership from Croatia and Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather, leaders of Herceg-Bosna. We never hesitated to sign anything, just as Franjo Tudjman never hesitated to put his signature on any peace proposal or truce put forward by any international body. Further on, the decision to recognise the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Immediately following the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the international community, the decision was adopted to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as an integral state. How can one explain this claim, then, that following the recognition there were territorial pretensions? Croatian Assemblymen waited for months to get on a plane and to go to Sarajevo to take up -- take up office there, the diplomatic office. The letter of President Mr. Franjo Tudjman addressed to Mr. Izetbegovic. Further on, please. We have a document here, instructions to all commanders, stating -- all commanders of Croatian army, stating that not a single commander of Croatian army is allowed to send troops outside the Republic of Croatia. All those who issue such orders will be held responsible. If there are any volunteers in Croatian units who are originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina and they wish to go to the battlefields and defend their homes, then the army commanders may not prevent them from doing that. Yes, I was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I had my family living there, and I had a natural right to go there and defend my homeland. The fact that I was a citizen of Yugoslavia meant that I was also a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was naturally entitled to go there. There are previous documents indicating that there were never more than 700 volunteers from Croatia in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The next fact that is frequently manipulated has to do with how many weapons were provided to Bosnia and Herzegovina. There are over 2.000 documents that went through this Tribunal dealing with this. Never, absolutely never was the supply with the weapons of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina interrupted. Those Mujahedin launching mortar shell, they received those weapons from Croatia. There was not a single occasion when the weapons were delivered to Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they did not go through the territory of Croatia with the approval of Croatia and with the assistance of Croatia. Everything they received they could only receive only through the territory of Croatia. Embargo banned all flights to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all the roads led through Croatia, through the territory referred to as Herceg-Bosna. In the history of wars, there was not a single similar instance. The commander of the HVO, the post held by me and General Petkovic, had to, wanted to and did let the weapons pass through, the weapons to the country which did what we saw them do. Never in the history of warfare did -- was any commander faced with such a difficult task. You will see over 2.000 documents here, all of them going to show that there was a continuous supply to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina going through our territory or with the assistance of our army. We helped distribute those weapons using humanitarian aid channels. They would take in Croatia cans, open them up, fill them up with ammunition, and then these cans were then sent to Visoko and other locations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was done continuously, even amidst most intensive fighting. Factory of ammunition -- factories of ammunition did not exist. And were they able -- if they were able indeed to manufacture anything, they needed raw materials, and these raw materials were supplied through the territory of Croatia. You can see a number of documents showing this. On the 7th of April, 1993, you see a document stating that the HVO approved the passage of so many bullets, and quantities of other weapons are indicated as well. This document shows that Rasim Delic, later on commander and later on indictee, playing the same role as we are here, distributes the weapons. At the time, he was in charge of logistics, so he distributes the weapons located in Grude, and he says so many weapons and so many millions of bullets are expected, and all of this is distributed in the following way. Then we turn to the next slide, bases and location in the Republic of Croatia from which weapons were supplied to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You see on the map the roads that were used for this supply. During this trial, Your Honours, you will receive a lot of evidence going to prove all of what I'm saying. All right. Let me repeat this in a calmer way. By way of documents and evidence, we will show to you that from all of these locations, continuously, throughout the entire course of war, weapons were sent to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We will turn to Bihac particularly. Small planes of ours flew to Bihac, and helicopters carrying blood supplies and all other necessary supplies. Everything they needed came exclusively from the Republic of Croatia. This was done in an organised fashion with the knowledge of the president of the republic, Minister Susak, myself, and everybody else who participated in this actively. Again the same thing, military representative offices of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Republic of Croatia, Zagreb, Split, and Rijeka. Can we see the document, please? Can we please study this document thoroughly? On the 12th of July, 1993, many crimes had already been committed against Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Still, on the 12th of July, this is what it says: "In order to perform duties from the -- within the purview of the staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the territory of the Republic of Croatia hereby we establish representative offices in the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb, Rijeka, and Split," and the names mentioned are all Muslim names; Osmanagic, and so on. When was it that a state in the history of warfare allowed the Main Staff of the army with which it was supposed to wage war which made an attempt to annex part of its territory, allowed the army that it was waging a war against to establish logistics bases, to establish training centres? Members of the BH army came from all over the place, from various countries; from Slovenia, from Germany where they worked, and in Zagreb at Borongaj, on Slume [phoen], Jastobacko [phoen], Plestovica, Kutina, Sisak, Jelnica, Djakovo. They would enter the barracks, and they would be trained to fight. They would be armed there, and they would be escorted to join the BiH army with which we had to wage a war down there with the consequences that we could all witness afterwards. In the Republic of Croatia, units of the BiH army were established. The following units: The 77th Brigade of the BiH army in Rijeka, the Berbir Brigade, the 17th Brigade, the Handzar Brigade. Whole units, brigades, were established and sent to join the BH army from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, with full knowledge of everybody. The Borovic Brigade, here we have names of all the members, which was 870 men strong. They all signed this document. They went to Visoko. They fought around Sarajevo. One part of that brigade went towards Srebrenica. Many of them died there. Some of them returned. They remained as officers of the Croatian army. They were pensioned from the Croatian army. For example, Colonel Porobic, who still resides in Rijeka in Croatia. This is the list of candidates for the training of specials, MUP specials from Sarajevo and other places. 460 of them, and I have not provided all the names, underwent specialist training in the Republic of Croatia. Once they were trained, once they were given weapons, once they were provided with communication means, they were sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Muslim people to the BiH army, to fight against the Serb aggression, because it is true that they were the biggest victims there. Can we go on, please, we've seen this. Can we see please the document. Can we please study the document that is before us. The Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina addresses the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, saying, "We would kindly ask you to allow for the stay in the Republic of Croatia for the following persons who were members of the anti-aircraft defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Follows a list of 22 names of pilots who were trained in the Republic of Croatia. They were accommodated there, they were fed there, and after the training they were returned to join the BiH army in order to try and prevent the destiny that awaited them and that would have awaited them if they hadn't been prepared in the way that they were. Next slide shows the situation with refugees. 402.000 refugees were in Croatia in December 1992, and there were 260.000 refugees from the Republic of Croatia. That number never went down below 195.000 refugees and 183 expelled persons. The table shows the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina and expelled persons from Croatia. This Trial Chamber and Prosecution has the means to verify every single piece of information that I'm going to present during this trial. At the beginning of 1996, Bosnia-Herzegovina had 2.960.000 inhabitants or one-half of the pre-war figures. 1.500.000 in the Federation and the rest in Republika Srpska. Out of them, 390.000 Croats or 52 per cent of the pre-war number of Croats that lived there before the war were in Bosnia-Herzegovina. 54 per cent were refugees. They were expelled from the Serbian territories. When the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina attacked them, again they expelled all the Croats and there are no Croats living there any more. What did we do with the hospitals and how we treated the injured and the wounded? All hospitals treated all the wounded. We did not pay any attention to the ethnic affiliation. Nobody ever asked anybody where they came from. Everybody from Bosnia-Herzegovina was taken care of and treated. These are the hospitals in Croatia. Not all the hospitals. These are only the hospitals that we analysed in Split-Firule, Krizine, Zagreb, Karlovac, Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci, Metkovic, Bosanski Brod and Krapinska-Toplica. Between all them they treated this many Muslim soldiers in 1992 through 1995: Split-Firule, 3.329. Altogether 10.623. We're talking about billions of dollars that were spent for the treatment of these people that were spent by a state that was in the war. One-third of its territory was occupied, its towns had been destroyed. There was no tourism or any other industry. There was an embargo on weapons. Over 10.000 people from Bosnia and Herzegovina, mostly Muslims, who were treated, who were looked after, who were taken care of, and we have the names of all of these people. What about the education system for the refugees? In 1992, the government of the Republic of Croatia, i.e., the Ministry for Education, passed a decision according to which the children of Muslim refugees in the Republic of Croatia were entitled to education and they should follow the curriculum that would be adapted to their national and cultural requirements. These are the schools in the Republic of Croatia that catered for the Muslims between 1992 and 1994. These children had special education in their own language, in the Bosnian language. Up to four lessons a week these children received to prevent them from losing their national and cultural identity in the Republic of Croatia. Here you can see the syllabus. You can see the cost of that education. The next slide shows humanitarian aid. All the humanitarian aid came via Croatia. Humanitarian aid in medicine for Muslims. These are the places which received from the hospital in Split medicines and medical supplies throughout the entire war. I'm talking about Srebrenica, Bratunac, and all the other places. Nobody ever asked whether this had to be paid, who had to pay for all of that, who needed that. Everything we had was distributed equally with full heart and without any misgivings. These are the Thank You notes that Muslim doctors sent to the Split hospital. There are over 40 of them, and we're going to show just a few. They're all signed, and you can see the Thank You notes by Muslim doctors, signed by them. Can we see the next one? And the next one. And the next one, please. These are the Thank You notes. Humanitarian aid between 1992 and 1995 went by different Croatian harbours; Rijeka, Pula, Split, Ploca. Unfortunately, our organisational capabilities were not such that it could provide us with all the documents, so I was only able to analyse the harbour Ploca. Over 580 million kilogrammes went via the harbour of Ploca. Both export and import. Exports from Bosnia of timber and the import of all the humanitarian aid. We have documents showing which ships entered the harbour, who the shipping agent was, and so on and so forth. I hope that in the course of this trial I will be able to analyse in the same manner the harbours of Rasa, Pula Rijeka, Split, and Trogir. You will see that the Intersped company of Bosnia-Herzegovina exported beach timber. This was a Bosnian company, and Intersped was exporting from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The diesel fuel was imported and it was distributed equally, and this will be proven by a number of documents. It was distributed in Mostar and elsewhere. One has to note here that everything that came from the Muslim states went only to Muslims. Western aid was distributed equally among all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A ship from Turkey brought weapons. We let the weapons through, but we stated that there were weapons in the ship and that those weapons were sent to Bosnia when we were fighting together and Muslims were manning some checkpoints or were standing guard. Between 1992 and 1995 in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, there were 234 foreign organisations for humanitarian aid originating from 32 countries, most of them from Muslim countries. In addition to local humanitarian organisations, these organisations were the most important factor for the aid to the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nobody ever had any problems with these organisations. Everything was open, and they did whatever they could. These are the addresses of all these organisations. You can find the lists of them. We only took one segment. The electric distribution system of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. My school colleague from grammar school was a Muslim who was in charge of electrical distribution in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had a degree in electrical engineering, and this is the scheme of electro-power plants in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This system could not function without the links being established with the electrodistribution system of Croatia. We provided them with electricity. They paid some of that but not all. Not for a moment did the Republic of Croatia think of stopping that supply although its system was on its knees. Never did the Republic of Croatia prevent the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats and Muslims alike, to have electricity. Whatever difficulties there were, they were of technical nature. When there was no electricity in Croatia, then there was no electricity in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nobody had it, neither Croats nor Muslims. Let's move on. Sport. One of the closest associates of Franjo Tudjman, the former vice-president of the Presidency of Croatia, is a member of the Olympic Committee, and since he had good ties with Mr. Samaranch, he managed to get Croatia enrolled in the Barcelona Olympic Games, although we had not been recognised by the United Nations, which was a precondition for us to participate. However, we did get the right to participate. He made a huge effort in order to get the team of Bosnia-Herzegovina to participate in Barcelona. The team of Bosnia-Herzegovina prepared itself in Istria at the expense of the Croatian taxpayer. How many of them we had at the time is a different issue. Once they were prepared, they got on a plane together with the Croatian athletes and they participated in Barcelona under a flag that was proclaimed the Bosnian flag which is no longer Bosnian flag. It was a Muslim flag. They participated in a flag featuring lilies. They were represented in a number of athletic disciplines. This is not a final -- final piece of information. I still don't have the final information. This is very important. In 1992, when it was still rather peaceful and there was still balance to a certain extent, to the extent possible, however, in 1993, during the Mediterranean Games in France, the war was still raging -- raging, and the Croatian state, despite the situation with the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the conflict with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, again prepared a team. Here there is just one team. In Croatia. They got on a plane, and they sent this team to France to participate in the games under their national flag. Your Honour, here we are facing a legal problem. The Mediterranean Games, unlike the Olympic Games, its participants are Mediterranean countries, and Bosnia-Herzegovina is a Mediterranean country owing to not more than 20 kilometres stretch of the coastal land between two Croatian cities. How is it possible to tell us that we want to confiscate that part of their territory and win it over for ourselves and at the same time we sent them to the Mediterranean Games as a Mediterranean team? Isn't this a legal recognition that this country does have an outlet to the sea, that this outlet to the sea is not in dispute? And all although this stretch of land is inhabited by 97 per cent of the Croatian population, it still is a legal confirmation that we do not have any aspirations to that stretch of land. These are the names of the people in the Bosnia-Herzegovina representation. We now move on to culture. I have not assembled a large volume of documents, but not a single artist from Bosnia and Herzegovina arrived in Zagreb without being looked after. A large number of them were issued with a passport by the Republic of Croatia in order to enable them to go to third countries without any problems and to earn their living. A friend of mine, a Croatian actor, Zlatko Vitez, who at the time was the minister of culture, the minister for culture of the Republic of Croatia, and if necessary he can testify here, can tell you how many people were issued with a passport and were not faced with any problems. Was Franjo Tudjman in charge of Stolac, Gornji Vakuf? That's very questionable. Was he in -- was he ruling over the groups and people there? Franjo Tudjman was -- presided over the organs of government of the Republic of Croatia. Weapons, recognition of the country, training of their men who wanted to fight. Four brigades, the MUP special purpose policemen, the refugees, the wounded, the humanitarian activity, education, culture, and sport, all of this was never brought into question. I assert that never in the history of warfare, and we have made a study of that area, has anything similar ever happened. Never has anybody assisted a people as much as the Croats assisted the Muslims in this war. No one ever anywhere. If I wanted to be malicious, I could ask how would it be possible for all of this to take place in the US after what al Qaeda did in New York? And yet that's what happened to us. How would it be possible in London after the SS and Wehrmacht aggression to help the German people in the same way as was done here? On the 11th of July, 1993, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued a communique after a meeting held in Zagreb. The communique itself is not important, but the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had a session in the city of Zagreb on the 11th of July, 1993. In a country which is now to be declared an aggressor against them? If there was an international conflict, then it was the other way round. It was the aggression of Bosnia and Herzegovina against Croatia. Why has all this happened? It's true that the Muslim people have suffered the most, that the worst crimes were committed against them, that the fate intended for them was the worst fate, that the people had the worst time in Sarajevo, that Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepca were overlooked and that silence was kept about them. But we are not to be blamed for that. Don't blame the Republic of Croatia. It was not our fault. Let me say that we did not participate in that. This is not to deny the fact that crimes occurred, that evil things happened, but this is clear evidence of the desires and the wishes. It wasn't just empty words. If we were to tape everything we say in our own homes for three days and then listen to that, we would find things to condemn. But these are facts. These are actions. This cannot be denied. Fifty thousand items of evidence have been handed over for translation here, and if it takes 15 years, let there be the courage to arrive at the truth, and we will arrive at it. We cannot agree to being a collateral victim because the death of a city was permitted, because genocide against a people was permitted. Let me read out something now. Mr. Clinton, the former president of the USA, in April 1992, the European Community accepted -- recognised Bosnia as an independent state for the first time since the 15th century. In the meantime, Serb paramilitary units continued to terrorise the Muslim people and kill the citizens, using the media all this time to convince the local Serbs that they were doing this as defence against the Muslims. On the 27th of April, Milosevic promulgated a new state of Yugoslavia consisting of Serbia and Montenegro. He then put on a show as if he were withdrawing his army from Bosnia while the weapons, the stockpiles, and the Bosnian Serbs were left under the command of Ratko Mladic. The fighting and the killing continued throughout 1992. The leaders of the European Community were estranged, and the Bush Administration was uncertain as to what to do and unwilling to get involved in new problems in an election year. Thus, they left the problem to be solved by the European Community. Even so, the Bush government interceded with the United Nations to have economic sanctions imposed on Serbia. This was a measure initially opposed by the Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the French and the British, who thought that Milosevic should be given a chance to stop the violence he had started. Finally, sanctions were finally imposed in late May, but to poor effect. The United Nations continued the arms embargo against the Bosnian government which was initially imposed on all of Yugoslavia in late 1991. The problem with the embargo was that the Serbs had enough weapons and ammunition to fight on for years. Therefore, the only consequence of keeping the embargo in place was to make it impossible for the Bosniaks to defend themselves. In the summer of 1992, television and the newspapers revealed the Serbian crimes in Northern Bosnia to Americans and Europeans, and I advocated NATO strikes. Later, when it became clear that the Serbs were carrying out a systematic massacre of the Bosnian Muslims, I proposed that the arms embargo be abolished. Instead of this, the Europeans focused on ending the violence. The British Prime Minister, John Major, intended to get Serbs to stop the siege of Bosnian towns and to put their weapons under UN supervision. The United Nations sent 8.000 soldiers to protect aid convoys. In other words, it's better for you to die with full stomachs than hungry. A little before the elections Lord David Owen, the European negotiator, and Cyrus Vance, the former US Secretary of State, presented a proposal, and so on and so forth. This has to do with cantonal governments. When I became president, the arms embargo and the European support to the Vance-Owen Plan weakened Muslim resistance to the Serbs even though the evidence of their massacres of civilians and human rights violations in prisoner of war camps came to light. In early February, I decided not to support the Vance-Owen Plan, and it fell through. On the 5th, I met with the Canadian Prime Minister, Brian Mulroney, and I was pleased to hear him say that he also did not like the plan. A few days later we completed a new plan for a Bosnian policy and Warren Christopher stated that the USA wished to negotiate a new agreement and that they were willing to support its implementation and so on. One did not agree to one thing, another did not agree to something else. One person was facing elections, another wanted to support Milosevic, and the massacre went on until Srebrenica. It was not the first or the last time. There are massacres still going on around us; in Africa, in Northern Ireland -- well, in Northern Ireland they finally stopped. In the Basque region in the heart of Europe, in Iraq, in Iran, Afghanistan, in the south of Africa, we have the Tutsis and the Hutus, the Chechens. Our moral fields, our moral values are obviously weak. We get excited when we see it happen, but then we soon forget. Therefore, in order to understand this entire story, apart from the facts and the numbers, it is important to understand what goes beyond the human reason. This is what Aristotle advises us to do. This is what extends our knowledge. We read novels and watch films so that we can live somebody else's life, the life of another character. We live one life in our own cultural environment in our own family and nation. Literature and art enable us to understand and experience the suffering on the Medusa raft, for example. If we are unable to do that, we will not be able to understand what happened there. We will not understand the state of mind. We will not understand what happened to young men who broke down, who had been normal young men. You saw those skinny youths. You saw those people stopping the tanks. These were the people who had to become soldiers overnight. It would have taken ten years to train them as soldiers. They were unable to understand overnight what order and discipline meant. They were not trained to know and understand what they could and couldn't do. When a friend of theirs was killed, or a colleague, some of them lost control. They broke down. And some of them would commit evil deeds. They were unable to give advance notice because they themselves didn't know they would do it. It could not be foreseen to fight against this, to explain. It makes more than issuing orders. It needs a lot of persuasion, a lot of love, a lot of understanding. And there was enough of that. There was a lot of that around. Croatia did nothing bad, according to this data. This country, which had so many refugees. And let me show you now some figures in comparison. Can we see these figures, please? I have created a simulated situation. France has 60 million inhabitants. I will round up the numbers. I've put France instead of Croatia here. It doesn't overlap completely, but I think you will understand what I'm trying to say. Let's look at this now. Aggression against France. Let's go on. This is the area of France that's occupied. Let's move on. If we take the proportions, occupied France in Croatia's situation has 4.992.000 people expelled, 4.553.000 refugees. I'm only now simulating. 151.000 have been killed. 351.000 Frenchmen wounded. 10.312 unknown persons have been killed. And French defenders, because of a distorted picture about the aggressor and the war and the desire to spread the guilt equally, 20.017 Croatian soldiers were killed. 10.000 mothers are still looking for the bones of their sons around Vukovar. Now let's look at the USA, for example. Imagine the next situation. France received 96.460 wounded from Bosnia and Herzegovina, 9.400.000 refugees, and 150.000 were killed. Look at the registered refugees and displaced persons in France by year. Look at the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have transposed the situation. If Bosnia and Herzegovina had the same number of inhabitants as France, and let's say 10.542.000 people were French rather than Croatian in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We shall see what this means, what the number of Croats killed means as against that number in France and the US. Let's look at a comparison with the USA. The USA would have had to receive 24 million displaced persons and 21 million refugees. We would have had 739.000 people killed. Thank God the USA had only 400.000 killed in World War II. However the number that would have been wounded would have been 1.715.000, and the number of suicides among war veterans would have been 97.000. Let's move on. Let's move on. This is what it would look like, more or less. Let's move on. The number of refugees registered in America by year. Let's move on. Same story. Let's move on. If Bosnia and Herzegovina had had the same number of Americans as there are in America, 51 million Americans would be living in Bosnia. Let's move on. So please look at these figures now. When we have 700.000 refugees in Croatia, it's like have 9.5 million in the USA. No, 9 million in France and 46 million in the USA. When we have 11.000 killed in Croatia, this would correspond to 151.000 in France and to 39.000 in the USA. When we have 26.000 wounded in France, it would be 351.000 and 1.715 wounded. When in Bosnia and Herzegovina we have 6.5 thousand Croats killed, it would correspond to 545.000 Frenchmen killed or to 2.661.000 Americans killed. Those who live in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The number of wounded from Bosnia and Herzegovina we looked after, 10.623 in Croatia, in France would proportionally have been 96.460 people, and in America 470.299. There is something called social psychology. I will skip over it because we're coming closer to the end of today's hearing and I will turn to something else. I have prepared some information here concerning the power outage in New York. Ten minutes after the power went out, over 2.000 stores, mostly those owned by Jews and white owners, were looted. A lot of people were killed. Thousands of people were arrested after that, and not tried. Let us now compare this to what happened after hurricane Katrina in a country that has the most powerful system to deal with it. When we look at unrest in France when the minister of the interior says a single word that the hooligans object to, we see how many millions of damage occur after that. We see how many people are injured. Can you imagine the situation in which a lot of your territory is occupied, a lot of your towns destroyed? At the same time you're changing your state and your economic system, and you're faced with such difficulties, what do you think? What results can a single person produce, or a government? And these results are impressive. We can now turn to the moral despair at the fact that we can do only so much. And there are also things that were done that we are ashamed of. However, pride and shame have to be distinguished, discerned. As we talk here, every 15 minutes a lot of children die, the same number of children as if a plane with 300 travellers was downed. It is shameful. I am shamed of what was done and committed by Croats, both in collection centres and in certain prisons. However, in none of those instances there was any intention to do that. But in addition to that, we also have a right to pride, because the efforts we invested with all of -- supported by all of this evidence and documents show that there was not a single parallel example in the history of warfare. When we take into account the number of UNPA zones under the control of the United Nations, 600 of people were killed in Croatia there. A lot of Serbs as well. And 400 Serbs were killed in revenge. These are terrible numbers. Every life lost is a terrible thing. However, if we remember 2 million of raped women in Germany, German women, these rapes were not committed only by Russians. If we remember, 120.000 raped women only in Berlin. If we also take into account then about 10.000 of them after this committed suicide. If we look at the situation in Iraq, if we take into account that about 2 million of Germans were killed in various collection sites throughout the war -- throughout the world after World War -- the Second World War, should we be ashamed of what happened in Croatia? Yes, we are ashamed of every individual crime. Every perpetrator needs to be prosecuted, but we have to identify these perpetrators. We have to locate them. The Prosecution here reminded me of the trial which took place before the French Revolution in 1789. While there were many irrational trials of witches, they would put their hands in hot oil, and if these women screamed, then they would be considered guilty, because the devil indicated that they were witches. If they didn't scream, then it was considered that the devil gave them strength to persevere. So either way you looked at it, these women were declared to be witches. And it seems here that the similar thing was done to us. I was supposed to flee from that country. I had to do what many fake intellectuals did to avoid responsibility. I should have fled. I should have found myself a cushy office and then issued statements from there. What did this mean, that we tried to play God? No. We have no attributes of God; however, the energy and the efforts we invested were tremendous. I would now like to show a film depicting my conduct. Not because I want to testify in my own defence, but I simply want to show you what certain situations looked like. Some of this is original footage and some is dramatisation where I hired actors to show you what it looked like in real life out in the field.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Humanitarian convoy was stopped in Citluk in Croatia. It was on its way to Mostar. This is out of control. This is beyond control. These are refugees from Central Bosnia. Mate Granic, minister of foreign affairs, he tried to mediate there. He spoke, but they didn't listen to him. You saw Mr. Prlic. He attempted the same. However, words were not enough here. These women had lost their children, their sons. Mate Boban tried to do something to ensure the passage of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Two hundred thousand besieged Croats need to receive up after four months food, medical supplies and so on." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We had to transport humanitarian aid via helicopters. We had to cooperate with Serbs in Kiseljak in order to ensure survivors. These are the children of refugees. These are not children from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Cedric Tolbert is here. He is another representative of the UN. But you can see that words were not sufficient under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] You have to listen to me. This is not about love. I was given eight trucks here this morning for Croatian people in Vitez. We need to transport this to Croats in Vares. We need to bring in nine bodies of dead people from Mostar. This is not about love. We have to save people up there. What happened, happened. The army will do its job. In order to feed Croats in Vares, in Zepca, in Vitez, we have to let this through. This is out of the question. Gentlemen, soldiers, remove these people here. The convoy needs to pass through. "Shut up and drive." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I wish to say one thing. If I remember, Mr. Scott, you said that this was a courageous act. No, it was not a courageous act. It was decisive act. One had to show pure force here. These are commanders. A chief of staff must not deal with civilians but that was the only way. There was no other way. One had to come in with full force every time. And I once apologised to the Honourable Chamber for doing so. I never boasted with anything in any interviews that I gave because that is not decent, but now that I am accused, I will remove this ban from myself. The courage, knowledge, energy and the time used. I'm not saying this to praise myself. I'm talking about this project. I don't know whose project it is, but I am dealing with this concept. I have been dealing with this concept for 40 years now. I don't know, whom should I thank for being brave and courageous. I don't know whether my height and stature have something to do with this, but I state to you now that nobody else in Europe in my shoes could have done more than I did. Now, let us play this film further.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The International Red Cross had arranged for a meeting to be held in the barracks in Capljina. Some people came to visit their children there, and once they started leaving, the others started shooting. The doctor I'm mentioning here is a Serb. His name is Moro. I started cursing here. I'm cursing here. I'm uttering terrible curses because he was firing from a sniper.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] These women are your mothers and children. Fuck your criminal mother." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Let this be interpreted for you because he was firing at the woman who was carrying a child in her arms. This woman was the wife of a JNA officer. I am standing in the middle of the street in the line of fire of this sniper. The cameraman didn't dare come closer to me. This was authentic footage that was never broadcast in Croatia due to my curses. What else was I supposed to do? How else was I supposed to plead with this man?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] You're a criminal. Fuck your Chetnik mother. You're a shit. These women are mothers and wives." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I was a commander. I had a certain area of responsibility, and I had to do this because otherwise he would have shot at them. The International Red Cross did their work. You can see how far they were from the sniper, because nobody would have taken responsibility for this. Had I not intervened, perhaps today I would have been held responsible for this. Look at the faces of these women. The men you see in a raincoat is a Serb. His son is a Serb, a doctor. The man to the right, the short one, is a Muslim who came to fetch his child. The second time they came, they started shooting ten metres in front of the barracks. I went there to get them, fully upright with all my height of a metre and 90 centimetres, I went there to the entrance to fetch them. I think I abbreviated my presentation as much as I could. I don't want to speak on behalf of the others, but we came to this Court voluntarily, and all we wish is to establish truth based on the facts. Let us see whether this movie footage that all of us played in our heads for hundreds of times and despite of all self-criticism I came to the point where I don't know what would I have done differently under the circumstances. What would you have done differently? To tell you the truth, I myself don't know. It seems to me, despite of all criticism, that I have done everything, absolutely everything. These are just details. We will hear lot more throughout two years. Petkovic had a pistol stuck in his mouth twice. Croats fired at him. All of these people were imprisoned. There were cases where Croats killed other Croats. We had dead people as a result of that. They fired above our heads. The only thing to do was either to flee or to get immersed into this with full energy, working 18, 20 hours a day, courageously, and see what could be done. We were ashamed of what we were unable to do, but I don't think that I ever attended a meeting or a gathering where with any of the people I met I heard anything that would be against my moral values, and I think that my moral values are fully proper, and I followed them throughout my life. We did not receive any transcript from the Croatian state enabling us to show everything that was said there. And these transcripts have a huge flaw. Tudjman says, for example, erroneously, "Pero Markovic, I know that," and there is no audio record of that to reflect it. I know. I myself know how this was said, how this was uttered, with what connotation. There are quotations taken out of context without showing you the entirety of all the facts. And if we pursue that line of presenting evidence, I am afraid we won't be able to reach the truth. It is my belief that after all of this, after thousands of documents, to speak of a joint criminal enterprise, Your Honours, I think insults elementary logic including legal logic. Such Croatia, such a conduct give no rise for such a conclusion. Whether we personally did everything in our abilities, whether we failed to do something due to our fatigue or the fact that we were overburdened, then yes, that could be investigated. That could be checked, and we stand ready to answer for such omissions. However, yes, it is possible to be guilty. It is human to err, and if that is the case, then we will serve honourably any sentence imposed on us. But I hope that we will have enough power and enough strength and enough courage, enough energy to establish the truth. Thank you for hearing me out. Thank you to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. You ended your opening statement within the time period that had been allotted to you. Thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber. This hearing is about to end. As you know, we shall resume the hearings next week. We have a holiday on Monday. Therefore, the next hearing is scheduled on Tuesday starting at 2.15 in the afternoon. Have a good rest until then and get ready for the next hearing. I hope that we shall then have a witness. Can you confirm this? I'm now turning to the Prosecution. He will be present in the courtroom. Fine. You're nodding that it is so. Let's hope that he's going to be here. Thank you. Let us convene again next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 25
